en: Some barrage designs generate on both the flood and the ebb, using the difference in both directions to make more of the daily tidal cycle.
A few designs pump extra water into the basin at high tide to enlarge the difference later, a method described in engineering reviews of tidal plants.
A storm surge is weather piled water, not the regular astronomical tide; sources for tidal energy must use tide tables, not typhoon water levels.
The Moon's gravity, with the Sun's, makes the tidal difference; secondary physics pages are the right source for why the water keeps rising and falling.
Before claiming a bay can make power, sources measure months of tide-gauge data; one afternoon of watching the shore is not a resource study.
Energy agencies also report high construction cost for barrages, so a suitable tide is necessary but not enough if the project cannot be paid for.
Modern source papers discuss fish passages and turbine slowdowns as ways to exploit tides while reducing harm to migrating animals.
Small island grids might use a modest tidal-stream unit if measurements show a reliable current, a situation different from a giant estuary barrage.
Because tides shift later each day, sources discuss whether generation times match evening demand, a siting question besides the size of the difference.
Barrage basins can trap sediment, shrinking the useful water difference over years, a long-term issue secondary environmental reviews flag.
A class investigation can start with a published tide table for a bay, then ask whether the listed high-low gap is large enough to interest an energy study.
Tidal energy is called renewable in textbooks because the Earth-Moon orbit keeps making the difference, unlike a coal pile that can run out.
Some coastal energy papers compare tidal sites with offshore wind; your task is still to identify the tidal-difference cases, not to switch topics to wind.
When you copy a site from a paper, write the typical tidal range in meters and the mean current speed, the two numbers that justify exploiting the difference.
The Bay of Fundy is often cited for an unusually large tidal range, a world example of a place where the difference is large enough to study for power.
A few technology reviews describe tethered tidal kites that fly in a current, another proposed way to exploit tidal-stream difference in deep channels.
National energy papers also mention permits for using a waterway, so a scientifically good tide still needs legal clearance to be exploited.
Secondary siting guides call for consulting fishing communities, because a turbine field can change the very channel people already use.
A proper study measures both spring and neap cycles so the smallest useful difference is known, not only the most dramatic high tide of the month.
Some tidal-stream designs use vertical-axis turbines that work with reversing current, matching a tide that flows two ways each day.
Other designs look like underwater wind turbines facing the current; sources still classify them as tidal-stream devices, not wind machines.
Engineering sources call the high-to-low water gap the tidal head; a larger head means more potential energy per cubic meter of water.
If the listed tidal head is only a few tens of centimeters, secondary sources usually drop the site, because turbines need a more useful difference.
One month of tide data can miss seasonal changes; energy papers prefer multi-year gauges before they call a difference exploitable.
A class can use a government energy outlook, a peer-reviewed siting paper, and a tide table, three secondary sources that together identify a possible site type.
Identifying a situation where tides could be used is not the same as promising a plant in your hometown; keep the claim as large as the source.
Some older barrages generate mainly on the ebb, releasing stored high water through turbines when the sea outside has already fallen.
Other schemes generate as the tide floods into a basin, another documented way of using the incoming height difference.
Marine energy reviews mention rust and biofouling on turbines, practical limits on exploiting a good tide that physics alone does not show.
Papers on tidal-stream farms discuss spacing turbines so the wake of one does not steal the current difference from the next.
